2.2.6 Use of Horizontal Drains in the United States

It appears from tne literature that more use is made of horizontal
drains for the control and prevention of landslides in the USA tnan
anywnere else in tne world. Horizontal drains were first used there for
the stapilisation of landslides in about 1939 (Smith & Stafford, 1957),
altnougn the metnod did not gain widespread acceptance until the early
1970's (Royster, 1977, 1980).

An early method of drain construction consisted of drilling a 50 m
diameter hole which was subsequently reamed out to 150 mm and cased with a
100 mm perforated metal pipe (Smitn & Stafford, 1957). It is reported by
Royster (1977, 1980) that, as drilling bit development proceeded, a 100 mn
modified fishtail bit was used to do the drilling in one operation, and a
50 mm vlack pipe casing, perforated with three rows of 10 mm holes at
75 mm centres at the quarter points, was used instead of the 100 mm
perforated metal pipe. He reported that over the years improvements in
drilling machines, materials and procedures have made the use of such
drains more attractive, tne most significant cnanges being the use of PVC
pipe as a liner for the drilled hole, heavy walled flush-coupled drill
rods, expandaole drag and roller oits and drilling machines capaple of
developing extremely high thrust and torque.

Royster (1977, 1980) outlined a frequently used installation
procedure whicn involves tne use of an expendaole roller or drag pit wnich
1s attached to the drill stem with a slotted adapter. Drill stem is added
in 3 m sections as tne hole is advanced. Water pumped at tne rate of
adout 2 litres/second is used to cool the bit and flush the cuttings from
tne nole. Once the required depth is reached, the pit is "knocked off' oy
reversing the direction of rotation of tne drill stem. Slotted PVC pipe
is tnen inserted tnrougn tne drill stem as it is extracted from the hole.
dorizontal drains more than 300 m long have been drilled using this
technique and equigment, and drains around 100 m in lengtn are commonly
drilled and cased during an eight nour shift (Smith, 1980).

Royster (1984) reported that the Tennessee Department of
Transportation nad installed several thousand feet of horizontal drains in
the past ten to twelve years. The maximum length of these drains was
183 m, these peing successfully installed in an emoankment composed of
nighly weathered shale with some sand and silt material (Royster, 1980).
Tne Tennessee Department of Transportation have found horizontal drains to
be apsolutely reliable and beneficial in most cases, provided that they
are tailored to suit the site conditions. They have not developed a
clean-out device or procedures for maintaining their installations, and
they rarely undertake any monitoring apart from visually observing
stability, as they do not have the time or the personnel to do this work.

Royster (1977, 1980) reported that the drilling machines used have
